title: Borrowing from a library of things
description: Many towns now lend tools, toys and kitchen gadgets like books, and borrowing suits the things we rarely use.

body.heading: The drill you need twice a year
paragraphs: Most households own things that work hard for one weekend and then sit in a cupboard for years: a drill, a carpet cleaner, a tall ladder, a chocolate fountain. A library of things, sometimes called a tool library, lends exactly these items for a small fee or membership.
Borrowing means someone else stores, maintains and repairs the item, and one well-used drill serves a whole street instead of gathering dust in twenty garages.

body.heading: Finding and using one
paragraphs: Search for tool libraries, sharing libraries or repair-and-share hubs in your area; some are run by councils, others by community groups or charities. Borrowing usually works like a book library: join, reserve, collect, return by the due date.
Treat borrowed items as you would a friend's: use them as intended, clean them before returning, and mention any problem honestly so it can be fixed before the next borrower.

body.heading: What borrowing teaches
paragraphs: Borrowing first is a useful pause before buying. Sometimes the borrowed version shows you exactly which features matter; sometimes it proves the urge passes and the purchase was never needed at all.

The same idea works informally. Neighbours who lend each other a hedge trimmer, a gazebo and a set of folding chairs have built a tiny library of things already, with friendship as the membership card.

takeaway: For things you need rarely, borrowing beats owning: cheaper for you, lighter on the cupboard, kinder to the planet.
